name: English for Everyday Life (ESL)
objectives: When you meet a new person, introduce yourself in English with your name, where you are from and what you do, and ask one question back, in at least three short sentences
When you do not understand what someone says, ask the person to repeat, slow down or spell a word with a polite English phrase, instead of pretending to understand
In a store, ask where an item is, ask the price and say how you will pay, using phrases from the lesson
At a doctor's office or on the phone, say what is wrong and make an appointment for a day and time that works for you, giving your name, the problem and the time, and repeating the time back
Given a place you need to go, ask for directions and repeat the directions back to check them, using direction words such as left, right, straight and next to

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Saying hello and introducing yourself
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Introduce yourself in three short sentences and ask one question back.
This lesson builds toward: When you meet a new person, you will introduce yourself in English with your name, where you are from and what you do, and ask one question back, in at least three short sentences.
When you meet someone new, start with a greeting: "Hello." or "Hi." In the morning you can say "Good morning." Then say your name: "My name is Ana." or "I'm Ana."
Add where you are from and what you do: "I'm from Guatemala." "I work at a restaurant." "I'm looking for a job." Then ask a question back: "What's your name?" "Where are you from?" When they answer, say "Nice to meet you."
Example conversation. A: "Hi, I'm Ana. What's your name?" B: "I'm Sam. Nice to meet you." A: "Nice to meet you too. I'm from Guatemala. I work at a restaurant." B: "Oh, which one?"
You do not need long sentences. Three short, clear sentences are a strong introduction. Smile, look at the person and speak a little slowly.
Step by step:
- Greet: "Hello." or "Good morning."
- Say your name: "My name is ..." or "I'm ..."
- Say where you are from: "I'm from ..."
- Say what you do: "I work at ..." or "I'm looking for a job."
- Ask one question back: "What's your name?" Then say "Nice to meet you."
Words to know:
- "I'm": a short way to say "I am".
- "Nice to meet you": a polite phrase you say when you meet someone for the first time.
- Introduce yourself: tell a new person who you are.
Official sources:
- USA Learns: free English courses for adults (Sacramento County Office of Education)
Try it now: Write your own introduction: your name, where you are from and what you do, in three short sentences. Add one question to ask back. Read it out loud three times. Then say it without looking at the paper.
You can now introduce yourself in three short English sentences and ask a new person a question back.

check.q: Someone says "Nice to meet you." What is a good answer?
check.why: "Nice to meet you too" is the polite answer when you meet someone.

check.q: Which introduction has a name, where you are from and what you do?
options: "I'm Ali. I'm from Somalia. I drive a truck."
check.why: It gives the name, the country and the work in three short sentences.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Asking someone to repeat, slow down or spell
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask a person to repeat, slow down or spell a word with a polite phrase.
This lesson builds toward: When you do not understand what someone says, you will ask the person to repeat, slow down or spell a word with a polite English phrase, instead of pretending to understand.
Everyone misses words sometimes, even native speakers. It is normal and polite to ask. It is much better than saying "yes" when you did not understand.
Useful phrases: "Sorry, can you repeat that, please?" "Can you speak more slowly, please?" "How do you spell that?" "What does that word mean?" "Can you write it down, please?"
To check that you understood, say it back: "So, Tuesday at 3 o'clock?" If you missed only one part, ask about that part: "Sorry, what time?"
Example conversation. A: "Your pickup is at the side entrance at four fifteen." B: "Sorry, can you speak more slowly, please?" A: "Side entrance. Four fifteen." B: "So, the side door at 4:15?" A: "Yes, that's right."
Step by step:
- Do not pretend to understand.
- Say "Sorry," and ask: repeat, slow down, spell or write it down.
- Say the important part back to check it.
- Wait for "Yes, that's right."
Words to know:
- "Repeat": say it again.
- "Slowly": not fast.
- "Spell": say the letters of a word one by one.
Try it now: Write the four phrases to ask for help on a small card and keep it in your pocket or phone. Read each one out loud five times. Then play a talk radio station or video, and each time you miss something, say one of the phrases out loud.
You can now ask someone to repeat, slow down, spell or write down a word, and say back what you heard to check it.

check.q: A worker talks very fast and you miss it. What do you say?
check.why: Asking the person to speak more slowly is polite and gets you the information.

check.q: The nurse says your doctor's name and you cannot write it. What do you ask?
check.why: "How do you spell that?" asks for the letters so you can write the name.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Shopping: finding things, prices and paying
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask where an item is, ask the price and say how you will pay.
This lesson builds toward: In a store, you will ask where an item is, ask the price and say how you will pay, using phrases from the lesson.
To find something, say "Excuse me" and ask: "Where can I find the rice?" or "Do you have diapers?" The worker may say "Aisle 5" (a numbered row in the store) or "Sorry, we're out of it."
To ask the price: "How much is this?" or "How much are these?" for more than one. At the register the cashier may ask: "Cash or card?" "Do you want a bag?" "Do you want your receipt?" Answer: "Card, please." "No bag, thanks." "Yes, please."
Keep your receipt. To bring something back, say: "I'd like to return this, please. Here is my receipt." Each store has its own return rules, so you can ask: "What is your return policy?"
Example conversation. A: "Excuse me, where can I find the milk?" B: "In the back, next to the eggs." A: "Thanks. How much is this?" B: "Three ninety-nine." A: "Okay. Card, please."
Step by step:
- Say "Excuse me" to get help.
- Ask "Where can I find ...?"
- Ask "How much is this?"
- At the register answer "Cash or card?" and "Do you want a bag?"
- Keep the receipt for returns.
Words to know:
- "Aisle": a row in a store with shelves on both sides. It sounds like "I'll".
- "Receipt": the paper that shows what you bought and paid. The p is silent.
- "Return": bring something back to the store for your money.
- "Cashier": the worker who takes your money at the register.
Try it now: Role play with a partner, or play both parts out loud: you are in a grocery store. Ask where two things are, ask the price of one, and answer the cashier's three questions. Next time you go shopping, use one phrase for real.
You can now ask where something is in a store, ask the price, answer the cashier and ask to return something.

check.q: You want to know the price of two shirts. What do you ask?
check.why: "How much are these?" asks the price of more than one thing.

check.q: The cashier asks "Cash or card?" What does she want to know?
check.why: "Cash or card?" asks how you will pay.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: The doctor, the phone and getting around

lessons.title: Lesson 4: At the doctor: saying what is wrong
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Tell a doctor or nurse what is wrong, where it hurts and for how long.
This lesson builds toward: At a doctor's office or on the phone, you will say what is wrong and make an appointment for a day and time that works for you, giving your name, the problem and the time, and repeating the time back.
At the front desk, say: "Hi, I have an appointment at 10 o'clock. My name is Ana Lopez." They may ask for your date of birth and your insurance card.
To say what is wrong: "I have a headache." "I have a fever." "My stomach hurts." "My back hurts." "I feel dizzy." Then say how long: "It started two days ago." or "I've had it since Monday." The doctor may ask: "Does it hurt here?" Answer: "Yes, there." or "No."
If you need help with English, you can ask: "Do you have an interpreter?" An interpreter is a person who helps you speak with the doctor in your language. Ask the doctor to write down instructions: "Can you write that down, please?" This course teaches words only. Questions about your health go to your doctor or nurse.
In an emergency, such as trouble breathing or chest pain, call 911 and say: "I need an ambulance." Then say where you are.
Step by step:
- At the desk: say your appointment time and your name.
- Say what is wrong: "I have a ..." or "My ... hurts."
- Say how long: "for two days" or "since Monday".
- Ask for an interpreter or for written instructions if you need them.
Words to know:
- "Appointment": a set day and time to see someone, like a doctor.
- "Fever": when your body is too hot because you are sick.
- "Interpreter": a person who helps two people talk in different languages.
- "Insurance card": the card from your health plan that the office asks to see.
Try it now: Practice only, with a made-up problem: write three sentences for the doctor, for example "I have a sore throat. It started on Sunday. It hurts when I swallow." Read them out loud. Then practice the front desk line with a made-up name and time.
You can now check in at the front desk, say what is wrong and for how long, and ask for an interpreter or written instructions.

check.q: Your head has hurt since yesterday. What do you tell the doctor?
check.why: It says the problem and how long it has lasted.

check.q: You do not understand the doctor well. What can you ask?
check.why: An interpreter helps you and the doctor understand each other.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Phone calls: making an appointment and calling the school
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make an appointment by phone and repeat the day and time back.
This lesson builds toward: At a doctor's office or on the phone, you will say what is wrong and make an appointment for a day and time that works for you, giving your name, the problem and the time, and repeating the time back. When you do not understand what someone says, you will ask the person to repeat, slow down or spell a word with a polite English phrase, instead of pretending to understand.
Phone calls are hard because you cannot see the person. Plan your words before you call and keep a pen and paper ready.
To make an appointment: "Hi, my name is Ana Lopez. I'd like to make an appointment, please." They ask: "What is it for?" "What day works for you?" Answer: "I have a cough." "Tuesday morning is good." Then repeat it back: "So, Tuesday the 12th at 9:30?" To change it: "I need to change my appointment, please."
To call your child's school when your child is sick: "Hi, this is Ana Lopez. My son, David Lopez, is sick today. He is in second grade. He will not come to school today."
If the call goes too fast, use your phrases from Lesson 2: "Sorry, can you speak more slowly, please?" "Can you spell that?" If they say a phone number, say it back in groups: "5-5-5, 0-1-2-3?"
Step by step:
- Write what you will say before you call.
- Say your name and why you are calling.
- Answer: what it is for, and what day and time works.
- Write the day and time, then say it back.
- End: "Thank you. Bye."
Words to know:
- "Make an appointment": set a day and time to see someone.
- "Change" / "cancel": move to a new time / stop the appointment.
- "What works for you?": a question that means "what day or time is good for you?"
Try it now: Write a short phone script to make a doctor's appointment, with a made-up name and problem. Role play it with a partner, or say both parts out loud. Make sure you repeat the day and time back at the end.
You can now make or change an appointment by phone, call your child's school, and repeat the day and time back to check it.

check.q: The office says "What day works for you?" What do they want?
options: A day that is good for you
check.why: "What day works for you?" asks which day is good for you.

check.q: The office says your appointment time. What do you do next?
options: Say the day and time back to check
check.why: Repeating the day and time back makes sure you heard it right.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Asking for directions
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask for directions to a place and repeat them back to check.
This lesson builds toward: Given a place you need to go, you will ask for directions and repeat the directions back to check them, using direction words such as left, right, straight and next to.
Start with "Excuse me." Then ask: "How do I get to the library?" or "Where is the bus stop?" or "Is the post office near here?"
Direction words: "Go straight." "Turn left." "Turn right." "It's on the corner." "It's next to the bank." "It's across from the park." "Go two blocks." A block is the part of a street between two corners.
Repeat the directions back: "So, go straight two blocks, then turn left?" The person will say "Yes" or fix it. If it is too much, ask: "Can you show me on my phone?" or "Can you point?"
Example conversation. A: "Excuse me, how do I get to the clinic?" B: "Go straight two blocks and turn right. It's next to the pharmacy." A: "So, straight two blocks, turn right, next to the pharmacy?" B: "That's right." A: "Thank you!"
Step by step:
- Say "Excuse me."
- Ask "How do I get to ...?" or "Where is ...?"
- Listen for left, right, straight, blocks and next to.
- Repeat the directions back.
- Say "Thank you!"
Words to know:
- "Straight": forward, without turning.
- "Block": the part of a street between two corners.
- "Across from": on the other side of the street from something.
- "Next to": right beside something.
Official sources:
- USA Learns: free English practice for adults
Try it now: Final task: make your Everyday English phrase card. Write your introduction, three phrases to ask someone to repeat or slow down, two store questions, a short phone script for a doctor's appointment, and one question to ask for directions to a place you go often. Read the whole card out loud, or role play it with a partner, and record yourself if you can.
You can now ask for directions, understand left, right, straight and next to, and repeat the directions back to check them.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Introduction Fewer than three sentences, or no name or no question back. Says name, where from and what they do, and asks one question back. Says it out loud without reading and adds one more detail, such as a goal. Asking to repeat or slow down No phrases, or the phrases are not polite. Three polite phrases to repeat, slow down, spell or write it down. Also shows how to say something back to check it, such as "So, Tuesday at 3?" Store questions No store questions, or they do not ask for an item or a price. Two clear questions, such as where an item is and the price. Also answers the cashier's questions in a role play. Phone script for an appointment Missing the name, the reason or the day and time. Gives name, reason, a day and time that works, and repeats the time back. Also shows how to change the appointment or ask for an interpreter. Asking for directions No question, or the question does not name a place. A clear question to a real place, and a sentence that repeats directions back. Uses three direction words correctly in a role play. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, practice that part and try again.

check.q: The person says "It's across from the park." Where is it?
options: On the other side of the street from the park
check.why: "Across from" means on the other side of the street.

options: "How do I get to the bus station?"
check.why: "How do I get to ...?" asks the way to a place.
